posts.subtitle: Don't panic. System Design interviews are open-ended discussions. This framework (Requirements, API, DB, Scale) will help you structure your answer.
posts.brief: System Design interviews are collaborative whiteboard sessions, not trick-question coding tests. Follow the framework — Requirements → Estimations → API → Data Model → High-Level Architecture → Deep-Dive — and you turn vague product ideas into defensible, production-ready designs.

posts.title: System Design Interview Basics: A Beginner-Friendly Framework for Clear Answers
posts.subtitle: A beginner-friendly way to structure requirements, estimates, diagrams, and trade-offs in your first design round.
posts.brief: System design interviews are not about inventing a perfect architecture on the spot. They are about showing a calm, repeatable process: clarify requirements, estimate scale, sketch a simple design, explain trade-offs, and improve it when constraints change.

posts.title: System Design Requirements and Constraints: Ask Better Questions Before You Draw
posts.subtitle: A practical framework for clarifying functional scope, non-functional targets, and trade-off boundaries in interviews.
posts.brief: In system design interviews, weak answers fail early because requirements are fuzzy. Strong answers start by turning vague prompts into explicit functional scope, measurable non-functional targets, and clear trade-off boundaries before any architecture diagram appears.

posts.title: The Role of Data in Precise Capacity Estimations for System Design
posts.subtitle: Don't guess. Calculate. We explain how to estimate QPS, Storage, and Bandwidth for your system de...
posts.brief: Capacity estimation is the skill of back-of-the-envelope math that tells you whether your system design will survive its traffic before you write a line of code. Four numbers do most of the work: **DAU, QPS, Storage/day, and Bandwidth/day**.

posts.title: System Design API Design for Interviews: Contracts, Idempotency, and Pagination
posts.subtitle: Design APIs interviewers trust by focusing on resource boundaries, request contracts, and failure-safe behavior.
posts.brief: In system design interviews, API design is not a list of HTTP verbs. It is a contract strategy: clear resource boundaries, stable request and response shapes, pagination, idempotency, error semantics, and versioning decisions that survive scale and failures.

posts.title: System Design Databases: SQL vs NoSQL and Scaling
posts.subtitle: The eternal debate: SQL or NoSQL? We break down ACID vs BASE, Sharding vs Replication, and when to use MongoDB vs PostgreSQL.
posts.brief: SQL gives you ACID guarantees and powerful relational queries; NoSQL gives you horizontal scale and flexible schemas. The real decision is not "which is better" — it is "which trade-offs align with your workload." Understanding replication, sharding, and the CAP theorem helps you pick correctly every time.

posts.title: System Design: Complete Guide to Caching — Patterns, Eviction, and Distributed Strategies
posts.subtitle: Cache-Aside to Refresh-Ahead, LRU to ARC — every caching pattern, eviction policy, and distributed strategy you need for system design
posts.brief: Caching is the single highest-leverage performance tool in distributed systems. This guide covers every read/write pattern (Cache-Aside through Refresh-Ahead), every eviction policy (LRU through ARC), cache invalidation pitfalls, thundering herd mitigations, multi-level topologies, and how Twitter, Netflix, and Facebook run caches at planetary scale. Read once; reference forever.

posts.title: System Design Sharding Strategy: Choosing Keys, Avoiding Hot Spots, and Resharding Safely
posts.subtitle: A practical guide to shard keys, routing, hot partitions, and how to scale storage without breaking queries.
posts.brief: Sharding means splitting one logical dataset across multiple physical databases so no single node carries all the data and traffic. The hard part is not adding more nodes. The hard part is choosing a shard key that keeps data balanced and queries practical.

posts.title: ID Generation Strategies in System Design: Base62, UUID, Snowflake, and Beyond
posts.subtitle: How to choose the right uniqueness strategy — from 6-char short URLs to distributed int64 order IDs
posts.brief: Short shareable IDs need Base62 (URL shorteners). Database primary keys at scale need time-ordered IDs (Snowflake, UUID v7). Security tokens need random IDs (UUID v4, NanoID). Picking the wrong strategy either causes B-tree fragmentation at 50M+ rows, production collisions, or IDs that leak your business metrics to competitors.

posts.title: Write-Time vs Read-Time Fan-Out: How Social Feeds Scale
posts.subtitle: The celebrity threshold, Redis sorted sets, and the hybrid model every social platform actually ships.
posts.brief: Fan-out is the act of distributing one post to many followers' feeds. Write-time fan-out (push) pre-computes feeds at post time — fast reads but catastrophic write amplification for celebrities. Read-time fan-out (pull) computes feeds on demand — no amplification but slow reads at scale. Production systems like Twitter/X, Instagram, and Facebook use a **hybrid**: write-time fan-out for users with ≤ 10K followers, read-time fan-out injected at read for celebrities above that threshold.

posts.title: System Design Networking: DNS, CDNs, and Load Balancers
posts.subtitle: The internet's traffic control system. We explain how DNS resolves names, CDNs cache content, and Load Balancers distribute traffic.
posts.brief: When you hit a URL, **DNS** translates the name to an IP, **CDNs** serve static assets from the edge nearest to you, and **Load Balancers** spread traffic across many servers so no single machine becomes a bottleneck. These three layers are the traffic control system of the modern internet.

posts.title: System Design Message Queues and Event-Driven Architecture: Building Reliable Asynchronous Systems
posts.subtitle: Design asynchronous pipelines with queues, retries, and consumer scaling that survive traffic spikes.
posts.brief: Message queues and event-driven architecture let services communicate asynchronously, absorb bursty traffic, and isolate failures. The core design challenge is not adding a queue — it is defining delivery semantics, retry behavior, and idempotent consumers.

posts.title: System Design Service Discovery and Health Checks: Routing Traffic to Healthy Instances
posts.subtitle: Learn how clients find services safely with registries, heartbeats, and health-aware load balancing.
posts.brief: Service discovery is how clients find the right service instance at runtime, and health checks are how systems decide whether an instance should receive traffic. Together, they turn dynamic infrastructure from guesswork into deterministic routing.

posts.title: System Design Replication and Failover: Keep Services Alive When a Primary Dies
posts.subtitle: A clear guide to replicas, failover detection, replica lag, and the trade-offs behind reliable database designs.
posts.brief: Replication means keeping multiple copies of your data so the system can survive machine, process, or availability-zone failures. Failover is the coordinated act of promoting a healthy replica, rerouting traffic, and recovering without corrupting data.

posts.title: System Design Observability, SLOs, and Incident Response: Operating Systems You Can Trust
posts.subtitle: Design telemetry, SLOs, and response playbooks that detect failure early and recover predictably.
posts.brief: Observability is how you understand system behavior from telemetry, SLOs are explicit reliability targets, and incident response is the execution model when those targets are at risk. Together, they convert operational chaos into measurable, repeatable decision-making.

posts.title: System Design HLD Example: URL Shortener (TinyURL and Bitly)
posts.subtitle: A senior-level HLD for a high-throughput short-link platform with 100:1 read-write ratio.
posts.brief: A URL shortener is a read-heavy system (100:1 ratio) that maps long URLs to short, unique aliases. The core scaling challenge is generating unique IDs without database contention—solved using a **Range-Based ID Generator** or a **Distributed Counter** with Base62 encoding. A 301/302 redirect strategy combined with aggressive Redis caching ensures sub-10ms response times.

posts.title: System Design HLD Example: Search Autocomplete (Google/Amazon)
posts.subtitle: Sub-10ms prefix lookup, ranking, typo tolerance, and language-partitioned indexes at Google scale.
posts.brief: Search autocomplete must respond in sub-10ms to feel "instant." The core trade-off is **Latency vs. Data Freshness**: we use an offline pipeline (Spark) to pre-calculate prefix-to-suggestion mappings and store them in **Redis Sorted Sets** (or a specialized Trie) for near-instant retrieval, while sacrificing real-time updates for most queries.

posts.title: System Design HLD Example: Distributed Cache Platform
posts.subtitle: Interview HLD for a distributed cache with eviction, invalidation, and resilience trade-offs.
posts.brief: Distributed caches trade strict consistency for sub-millisecond read latency, using consistent hashing to scale horizontally without causing database-shattering "cache stampedes" during cluster rebalancing.

posts.title: System Design HLD Example: News Feed (Home Timeline)
posts.subtitle: Interview-focused HLD for a scalable social feed with fan-out and ranking trade-offs.
posts.brief: A news feed system builds personalized timelines by combining content publishing, graph relationships, and ranking. The scalability crux is the fan-out amplified write path: a single celebrity post can trigger 100M writes. A hybrid fan-out strategy—push for normal users, pull for celebrities—is the industry standard for 99.99% availability.

posts.title: System Design HLD Example: Payment Processing Platform
posts.subtitle: An interview-ready HLD for payments focusing on correctness, idempotency, and recovery.
posts.brief: Payment systems optimize for correctness first, then throughput. This guide covers idempotency, double-entry ledgers, and reconciliation.

footerPosts.title: Adapting to Virtual Threads for Spring Developers
footerPosts.subtitle: Migrate your Spring Boot services from thread-pool exhaustion to JDK 21 virtual threads — the practical Spring developer guide
footerPosts.brief: Platform threads (one OS thread per request) max out at a few hundred concurrent I/O-bound requests. Virtual threads (JDK 21+) allow millions — with zero I/O-blocking cost. Spring Boot 3.2 enables them with a single property. Avoid `synchronized` blocks wrapping I/O (they pin virtual threads to OS threads) and CPU-bound work inside virtual threads. For I/O-heavy Spring services, virtual threads are the most impactful JVM upgrade since Java 8 lambdas.

footerPosts.title: ACID Properties Explained: How SQL Databases Guarantee Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability
footerPosts.subtitle: A deep dive into PostgreSQL WAL logs, MVCC snapshot isolation, Write Skew anomalies, and crash recovery
footerPosts.brief: Trace how storage engines process high-stakes financial transactions like bank transfers using Write-Ahead Logging (WAL), Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC), and SSI locks without data loss or corruption.

footerPosts.title: ACID Transactions in Distributed Databases: DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, and Spanner Compared
footerPosts.subtitle: How modern NoSQL databases achieve atomicity and isolation without a single machine
footerPosts.brief: ACID transactions in distributed databases are not equal. DynamoDB provides multi-item atomicity scoped to 25 items using two-phase commit with a coordinator item, but only within a single region. Cosmos DB wraps partition-scoped operations inside a stored procedure using a JavaScript continuation model — cross-partition writes get no atomic guarantee. Google Spanner is the only cloud database that delivers true global ACID with external consistency, using TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks) to assign globally ordered timestamps and a commit-wait delay to guarantee causality across datacenters. MongoDB supports multi-document transactions on replica sets but carries measurable performance overhead and does not prevent write skew under snapshot isolation. The right choice depends on atomicity scope, latency tolerance, and operational cost — not on which database claims to be "ACID-compliant."

footerPosts.brief: Large Language Models are brilliant "brains in a jar." Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) hands them a constantly refreshed memory, while AI Agents give them tools to act in the world. Combined, they turn static knowledge into dynamic, goal-directed intelligence — the next frontier of practical AI.

footerPosts.subtitle: Production AI needs explicit routing, memory, execution, and evaluation layers rather than one loop.
footerPosts.brief: A single agent loop is enough for a demo, but production AI systems need explicit layers for routing, execution, memory, and evaluation. Those layers determine safety, latency, cost, and traceability far more than model choice alone.

footerPosts.subtitle: Master shortest paths, dependency resolution, and cycle detection with robust Java solutions.
footerPosts.brief: Graph algorithms are the backbone of networking, scheduling, and connection analysis. This guide explores Dijkstra's pathfinding, Topological Sorting for dependency resolution, and Disjoint Set Union (DSU) for cycle detection, complete with runnable Java code.

footerPosts.title: AI Agents Explained: When LLMs Start Using Tools
footerPosts.subtitle: An LLM can talk, but an AI Agent can *act*. We explain how Agents use the ReAct framework to brow...
footerPosts.brief: A standard LLM is a brain in a jar — it can reason but cannot act. An **AI Agent** connects that brain to tools (web search, code execution, APIs). Instead of just answering a question, an agent executes a loop of Thought → Action → Observation until the goal is reached.

footerPosts.title: ANN Index Types Explained: When to Choose Flat, HNSW, IVF, or IVF-PQ
footerPosts.subtitle: A production-first guide to picking the right vector index for recall, latency, memory, and update patterns.
footerPosts.brief: If your dataset is small and correctness is critical, use Flat. If you need high recall with low latency and enough RAM, use HNSW. If your corpus is huge and memory is your bottleneck, use IVF-PQ. Start with HNSW for most RAG systems, then move to IVF or IVF-PQ when scale and cost force compression.

footerPosts.subtitle: Process petabytes with Python: understand Spark's execution model, DataFrame transformations, partitioning strategy, and real-time streaming.
footerPosts.brief: Apache Spark distributes Python DataFrame jobs across a cluster of executors, using lazy evaluation and the Catalyst query optimizer to process terabytes with the same code that works on gigabytes. Master partitioning, shuffle-awareness, and Structured Streaming and you have a single engine for both batch and real-time pipelines.

footerPosts.title: Attention Mechanism Explained: How Transformers Learn to Focus
footerPosts.subtitle: From the query-key-value formulation to multi-head attention — the mechanism that made transformers dominate AI
footerPosts.brief: Attention lets every token in a sequence ask "what else is relevant to me?" — dynamically weighting relationships across all positions simultaneously. It replaced the fixed-size hidden-state bottleneck of RNNs and is the engine behind every GPT, BERT, ViT, and AlphaFold model you have ever used.

footerPosts.title: API Gateway vs. Load Balancer vs. Reverse Proxy: What's the Difference?
footerPosts.subtitle: They all sit in front of your servers. But do you need Nginx, HAProxy, or Kong? We clarify the roles of each component.
footerPosts.brief: A **Reverse Proxy** hides your servers and handles caching/SSL. A **Load Balancer** spreads traffic across server instances. An **API Gateway** manages API concerns — auth, rate limiting, routing, and protocol translation. Modern tools (Nginx, AWS ALB, Kong) often combine all three, but understanding what each layer does independently is essential for system design.

The **Backend for Frontend (BFF)** pattern solves this by creating a dedicated API server for each client type — the mobile BFF reshapes data for small screens, the web BFF aggregates for dashboards.

footerPosts.subtitle: Backtracking is a brute-force algorithmic technique that solves problems by trying to build a sol...
footerPosts.brief: Backtracking is "Recursion with Undo." You try a path, explore it deeply, and if it fails, you **undo** your last decision and try the next option. It explores the full search space but prunes invalid branches early, making it far more efficient than brute force.

footerPosts.subtitle: Choose ingestion, serving, and ownership patterns deliberately when data platforms start to scale.
footerPosts.brief: A serious data platform is defined less by where files are stored and more by how changes enter the system, how serving layers are materialized, and who owns quality over time. Lambda, Kappa, CDC, Medallion, and Data Mesh are patterns for making those choices explicit.

footerPosts.title: Big Data 101: The 5 Vs, Ecosystem, and Why Scale Breaks Everything
footerPosts.subtitle: Why traditional databases fail at scale, what the 5 Vs really mean, and a practical map of the big data ecosystem from ingestion to insights.
footerPosts.brief: Traditional databases fail at big data scale for three concrete reasons — storage saturation, compute bottleneck, and write-lock contention. The 5 Vs (Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value) frame what makes data "big." A layered ecosystem — Kafka for ingestion, S3 for storage, Spark for processing, Snowflake for serving — assigns one tool per failure mode.

footerPosts.title: Exploring Different Types of Binary Trees
footerPosts.subtitle: Not all Binary Trees are created equal. We explain Full, Complete, Perfect, and Balanced Binary T...
footerPosts.brief: A Binary Tree has at most 2 children per node, but the **shape** of the tree determines performance. A **Full** tree has 0 or 2 children. A **Complete** tree fills left-to-right. A **Perfect** tree is a symmetric triangle. A **Degenerate** tree becomes a linked list with $O(N)$ search.

footerPosts.title: Big O Notation Explained: Time Complexity, Space Complexity, and Why They Matter in Interviews
footerPosts.subtitle: Master Big O notation: measure algorithm efficiency from O(1) to O(n²) with growth diagrams, worked examples, and the interview mental model.
footerPosts.brief: Big O notation describes how an algorithm's resource usage *grows* as input size grows — not how fast it runs on your laptop. Learn to identify the 7 complexity classes (O(1) through O(n!)), derive time and space complexity by counting loops and stack frames, and communicate your analysis in three sentences that satisfy any FAANG interviewer.

footerPosts.title: Binary Search Patterns: Five Variants Every Senior Engineer Knows
footerPosts.subtitle: Binary search has five distinct patterns — classic, leftmost, rightmost, rotated arrays, and 2D matrices.
footerPosts.brief: Binary search has five patterns beyond the classic "find the target": leftmost position, rightmost position, rotated array search, minimum in rotated array, and 2D matrix search. The root of every off-by-one bug is a mismatched loop condition and boundary update. Learn the invariant for each pattern and you will never write a broken binary search again.

## Stage 1 — What Makes a Strong System Design Response

- Before diving into the framework, understand what separates a strong response from a weak one.
- Weak responses jump straight to a specific technology ("I'd use Kafka and Cassandra") before understanding requirements.
- They treat the problem as a trivia question with a known answer.
- Strong responses start by asking clarifying questions, establish constraints with back-of-envelope estimates, and justify every decision with explicit trade-offs.

## Stage 3 — Key Mechanics: Caching, Fan-out, and Hot Users

- Caching the feed Each user's feed is stored in Redis as a sorted set, where the tweet ID is the member and the tweet's creation timestamp is the score.
- This structure makes inserting a new tweet O(log N) and retrieving the most recent top-N tweets equally fast — both well within the sub-10 ms latency budget of a production feed service.
- The score-based ordering also enables cursor-based pagination naturally: slide the score window backward in time to fetch the next page without offset scanning.
- Fan-out strategies Hot user problem: A celebrity with 50 M followers cannot push-fan-out on write without overloading the system.

## Scenario context

System design interviews are not about inventing a perfect architecture on the spot. They are about showing a calm, repeatable process: clarify requirements, estimate scale, sketch a simple design, explain trade-offs, and improve it when constraints change.

- Most beginners think a system design interview is a test of memory.
- They assume they must instantly recall the "right" architecture for a URL shortener, chat app, or news feed.
- That is the wrong mental model.

**Concepts in play:** system-design-hld-architectures, caching, api-gateway, consistency-replication

## Stage 1 — The Three Beginner Moves Before You Draw Anything

- Before any diagram, API, or storage choice, make three moves.
- Ask what the user can do and what the system does not need to do.
- If the prompt is "Design Instagram," you do not need to design every feature on Earth.
- You might narrow the scope to posting photos, following users, and loading a home feed.

## Stage 2 — The 30-Minute Whiteboard Flow That Keeps You Organized

- Once you have the scope, use a simple flow for nearly every interview.
- Estimate rough scale with quick capacity estimation math.
- Identify the core entities and APIs with explicit API contract design and data modeling choices.
- Sketch a high-level architecture.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Sketch a high-level architecture.

## Stage 3 — Real-World Application: Designing a Tiny URL Shortener in an Interview

- A URL shortener is one of the best beginner interview exercises because the problem is small enough to explain clearly but still exposes real design trade-offs.
- Start with the simplest product definition: - A user submits a long URL.
- - The system returns a short code.
- - Anyone with that short code can redirect to the original URL.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

- If the interviewer asks you to design a rate limiter, do not start by naming Redis and token buckets immediately.
- Start with the shape of the problem.
- Is the limit per user, per IP, per API key, or per endpoint?
- Is it 100 requests per minute or 1,000 per second?

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

- The application uses the cache-aside pattern for reads — checking Redis first and falling back to the database on a miss, then populating Redis so the next request is served from cache.

articles.title: The Role of Data in Precise Capacity Estimations for System Design
articles.contentMarkdown:
## Scenario context

Capacity estimation is the skill of back-of-the-envelope math that tells you whether your system design will survive its traffic before you write a line of code. Four numbers do most of the work: **DAU, QPS, Storage/day, and Bandwidth/day**.






```mermaid
flowchart LR
    DAU["Daily Active Users (e.g., 10M)"] --> QPS["Convert to QPS (requests/sec)"]
    QPS --> Storage["Storage/day (data written)"]
    QPS --> Ba…

This walkthrough focuses on **Reference Numbers to Memorize**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- 

**Concepts in play:** system-design-hld-architectures, caching, jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection, consistency-replication

## Stage 1 — Estimation Decision Flow

- Use this decision tree to structure any capacity estimation from scratch.
- Start with DAU and follow the branches to determine what infrastructure tier your system actually needs — single server, horizontally scaled, or fully distributed.
- The key decision point is the scale tier .
- A system handling 100 RPS and one handling 100,000 RPS require fundamentally different architectures — not just bigger servers, but different data stores, caching strategies, and deployment models.

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start[Start Estimation] --> DAU[Estimate DAU]
    DAU --> RW[Estimate Read/Write Ratio]
    RW --> QPS[Calculate QPS DAU  actions / 86400]
    QPS --> Peak[Multiply by 2-3x for peak]
    Peak --> Storage[Calculate Storage/day write QPS  record size  86400]
    Storage --> BW[Calculate Bandwidth read QPS  response size]
    BW --> Scale{Scale tier?}
    Scale -->|< 1000 RPS| Small[Single server PostgreSQL]
    Scale -->|1k-100k RPS| Med[App servers + cache + sharding]
    Scale -->|> 100k RPS| Large[Distributed system CDN + microservices]
```

**Observable outcome:** A system handling 100 RPS and one handling 100,000 RPS require fundamentally different architectures — not just bigger servers, but different data stores, caching strategies, and deployment models.

## Stage 2 — Real-World Application: Capacity Estimation Across Scale Tiers

- The best way to internalize the four-step pipeline is to run it on systems you already use every day.
- Here are three scenarios at very different scales that demonstrate how the numbers drive architecture decisions.
- Twitter/X-Scale Feed - DAU: 400M users.
- Each user reads ~10 timeline requests/day; each user writes ~0.1 tweets/day.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Each user reads ~10 timeline requests/day; each user writes ~0.1 tweets/day.

## Stage 3 — Deep Dive: Worked Example — Design a Pastebin

- - Write QPS = (1M × 1 paste/day) / 86400 ≈ 12 writes/sec - Read QPS = 12 × 10 = 120 reads/sec - Storage: 12 writes/sec × 10 KB × 86400 = ~10 GB/day → 10 TB over 3 years.
- - Read bandwidth: 120 reads/sec × 10 KB = 1.2 MB/sec → no CDN needed at this scale.
- What this tells you: - A single PostgreSQL can comfortably handle sub-1000 writes/sec.
- - Storage backend should be durable object storage to handle 10 TB over 3 years.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** - Storage backend should be durable object storage to handle 10 TB over 3 years.

## Stage 4 — Practical: Interview Estimation Template

- In a system design interview, the interviewer is watching whether you have a structured process — not whether you arrive at the exact right number.
- Here is a reusable five-step template you can follow verbatim: Quick Reference Decision Rules Two threshold rules that short-circuit most infrastructure architecture debates: - If storage 1 TB/day → use object storage (…
- A relational database is not designed for multi-terabyte raw ingest at sustained write rates.
- - If read bandwidth 1 GB/s → put a CDN in front.

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

```
Step 1 — State assumptions:
  - DAU: X million
  - Read:Write ratio: X:1
  - Average object size: X KB/MB

Step 2 — Calculate QPS:
  - Write QPS = DAU × writes_per_user / 86400
  - Read QPS = Write QPS × read_write_ratio
  - Peak QPS = Average QPS × 3

Step 3 — Calculate Storage:
  - Storage/day = write QPS × record_size × 86400
  - 5-year storage = storage/day × 365 × 5
  - Account for replication: × 3

Step 4 — Calculate Bandwidth:
  - Read bandwidth = read QPS × response_size
  - CDN threshold: > 1 GB/s read bandwidth

Step 5 — Determine scale tier:
  - < 1k RPS: single server
  - 1k-100k RPS: horizontal scaling + cache
  - > 100k RPS: distributed + CDN
```

**Observable outcome:** - If read bandwidth 1 GB/s → put a CDN in front.

## Stage 5 — Spring Boot + JMeter: From Capacity Estimates to Measured Throughput

- Spring Boot is the standard Java framework for building the HTTP services whose QPS, storage, and latency you estimate.
- Apache JMeter is the open-source load testing tool that validates those estimates against a running service — generating synthetic traffic at the calculated peak load and measuring actual throughput and p95 latency.
- The workflow: estimate peak QPS on paper → implement the endpoint → run a JMeter test plan at estimated load → compare results against your SLA targets.
- Instrument the endpoint to compare live p95/p99 against your paper estimate: JMeter test plan — simulating estimated peak load: Capacity estimate vs.

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

```java
// Close the estimation feedback loop: @Timed captures actual latency from live traffic
// so you can compare measured p95 against the "p95 < 50ms at 11,600 RPS" estimate.

@GetMapping("/api/users/{id}")
@Timed(value = "user.lookup.latency",
       percentiles = {0.50, 0.95, 0.99},    // exported to Prometheus/Grafana/Actuator
       description = "Cache-aside: Redis ~0.5ms hit, DB ~5ms miss")
public ResponseEntity<UserDto> getUser(@PathVariable String id) {
    // L1 — Redis: serves ~90%+ of requests at sub-millisecond cost
    UserDto cached = cache.opsForValue().get("user:" + id);
    if (cached != null) return ResponseEntity.ok(cached);

    // L2 — PostgreSQL: cache miss, fills cache for next request (5-minute TTL)
    return userRepository.findById(id)
        .map(u -> { cache.opsForValue().set("user:" + id, u, 5, MINUTES); return ResponseEntity.ok(u); })
        .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
}
// If Actuator shows p99 > 100ms → add a read replica or extend Redis TTL
```

```xml
<!-- Thread Group: 1000 concurrent users, 5-minute sustained load at peak QPS -->
<!-- This maps to: 11,600 RPS ÷ 1000 users ≈ 11.6 requests/sec per user -->
<ThreadGroup>
  <numThreads>1000</numThreads>         <!-- virtual users -->
  <rampTime>60</rampTime>               <!-- ramp up over 60 seconds -->
  <duration>300</duration>              <!-- hold load for 5 minutes -->

  <HTTPSamplerProxy>
    <domain>localhost</domain>
    <port>8080</port>
    <path>/api/users/${userId}</path>   <!-- CSV Data Set: randomised user IDs -->
    <method>GET</method>
  </HTTPSamplerProxy>

  <!-- Add Listeners: Aggregate Report, Response Time Graph, Active Threads Graph -->
</ThreadGroup>
```

**Observable outcome:** Instrument the endpoint to compare live p95/p99 against your paper estimate: JMeter test plan — simulating estimated peak load: Capacity estimate vs.

## Stage 6 — Key Lessons from Back-of-Envelope Estimation

- Five lessons that separate engineers who nail capacity estimation from those who overcomplicate it: 1.
- The goal is the scale tier, not the exact number.
- Whether your estimate lands at 80,000 RPS or 120,000 RPS doesn't change the architecture decision: both require distributed infrastructure with a load balancer and horizontal scaling.
- A 10× error is usually tolerable; a 100× error is a design problem.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start[Start: State Assumptions] --> DAU[DAU  actions/user]
    DAU --> QPS[Avg Write QPS = DAU  writes / 86400]
    QPS --> Peak[Peak QPS = Avg  2-3x]
    Peak --> RQPS[Read QPS = Write QPS  read: write ratio]
    RQPS --> Storage[Storage/day = write QPS  record size  86400]
    RQPS --> BW[Bandwidth/day = read QPS  response size]
    Storage --> Scale{Scale tier?}
    BW --> CDN{BW > 1 GB/s?}
    CDN -->|Yes| AddCDN[Add CDN layer]
    CDN -->|No| NoCDN[Direct serving OK]
    Scale -->|under 1k RPS| Small[Single server]
    Scale -->|1k-100k RPS| Med[Horizontal + cache]
    Scale -->|over 100k RPS| Large[Distributed + CDN]
```

**Observable outcome:** A 10× error is usually tolerable; a 100× error is a design problem.

## End-to-end outcome

The Role of Data in Precise Capacity Estimations for System Design

## Alternatives considered

The source focuses on one primary design. A second architecture is not compared, so no alternative is invented here.

## Failure and degraded modes

### Trade-offs & Failure Modes: Trade-offs, Failure Modes & Decision Guide: Estimation Mistakes

- **Detection:** Trade-offs & Failure Modes: Trade-offs, Failure Modes & Decision Guide: Estimation Mistakes
- **User or operator impact:** Trade-offs & Failure Modes: Trade-offs, Failure Modes & Decision Guide: Estimation Mistakes

articles.title: System Design API Design for Interviews: Contracts, Idempotency, and Pagination
articles.contentMarkdown:
## Scenario context

In system design interviews, API design is not a list of HTTP verbs. It is a contract strategy: clear resource boundaries, stable request and response shapes, pagination, idempotency, error semantics, and versioning decisions that survive scale and failures.

> **TLDR**: Good API design reduces ambiguity for clients and prevents operational incidents when traffic grows.

In 2015, Stripe renamed the `amount` field to…

This walkthrough focuses on **Why API Design Is an Architecture Decision, Not a Syntax Exercise**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- In 2015, Stripe renamed the amount field to amount cents in their charge response object — a clarification that made semantic sense internally.
- They had an active changelog and sent developer notifications.
- It still silently broke integrations for hundreds of third-party apps and payment platforms that parsed the response without strict field validation.

**Concepts in play:** system-design-hld-architectures, caching, git-internals-and-versioning, api-gateway

## Stage 1 — The API Contract Checklist You Should Apply in Every Interview

- You can use a reusable checklist to keep API design systematic.
- Define the resource model and identifiers.
- Define the core operations per resource.
- Define request and response fields with explicit constraints.

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Define request and response fields with explicit constraints.

## Stage 2 — Deep Dive: Translating Product Behavior Into Stable API Contracts

- API contracts are where product semantics become system boundaries.
- The Internals: Validation, Idempotency Store, and Backward Compatibility At runtime, robust API services usually implement these internal mechanisms: - Request validation layer for schema and semantic rules.
- - Idempotency key store for safe retried writes.
- - Serialization logic with explicit field defaults.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** - Serialization logic with explicit field defaults.

## Stage 3 — API Lifecycle Flow From Client Request to Stable Response

- This flowchart captures the API contract philosophy: consistent validation, safe retries, and predictable responses.
- 📊 REST API Request Lifecycle This sequence diagram traces the full lifecycle of a single REST API request from the client through the gateway and into the order service, highlighting the idempotency key check and the d…
- The flow shows that the API gateway handles cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate limiting) while the service layer owns business validation and deduplication.
- Take away: every hop in this chain is an opportunity for failure, which is why idempotency at the service boundary prevents duplicate side effects from network retries.

*Applies **git-internals-and-versioning** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Client request] --> B[Schema and semantic validation]
    B --> C{Idempotency key present?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Check idempotency store]
    D --> E{Seen before?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Return previous response]
    E -->|No| G[Execute business transaction]
    C -->|No| G
    G --> H[Persist result and emit event]
    H --> I[Return structured response]

```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant G as API Gateway
    participant S as Order Service
    participant DB as Database
    C->>G: POST /v1/orders
    G->>G: Auth and rate limit
    G->>S: Forward request
    S->>S: Validate schema
    S->>DB: Check idempotency key
    DB-->>S: Key not found
    S->>DB: Write order record
    DB-->>S: Commit OK
    S-->>G: 201 Created
    G-->>C: 201 + order_id

```

**Observable outcome:** Take away: every hop in this chain is an opportunity for failure, which is why idempotency at the service boundary prevents duplicate side effects from network retries.

## Stage 4 — Real-World Applications: Payments, Feeds, and Internal Microservices

- Payments API: idempotency is non-negotiable because duplicate charges are business-critical incidents.
- Timeline/feed API: pagination and filtering matter most, because reads dominate and data size grows continuously.
- Internal microservice APIs: strict schemas, backward compatibility, and explicit error contracts reduce coordination cost between teams.
- Different domains stress different contract dimensions, but the checklist remains stable.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Different domains stress different contract dimensions, but the checklist remains stable.

## Stage 5 — Practical Example: Design a Create-and-List Orders API

- Suppose your interview prompt includes order creation and order history.
- You can propose: - POST /v1/orders with idempotency key.
- - GET /v1/orders/{order id} for direct lookup.
- - GET /v1/orders?customer id=...&cursor=...&limit=...

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** - GET /v1/orders?customer id=...&cursor=...&limit=...

## Stage 6 — Self-Documenting API Contracts: Design Approach

- A production REST API benefits from machine-readable contract documentation that stays in sync with the implementation.
- The key principle is that the contract specification should be derived from the code rather than maintained as a separate manual artifact — ensuring that the documented API always matches what the service actually does.
- In practice, this means annotating each endpoint with its intended summary, description, request parameters, and expected response codes at the point of definition.
- A create-order endpoint would declare that it accepts an idempotency key header, requires a valid request body, and returns 201 on success, 409 on duplicate key conflict, 429 on rate limit, and 422 on malformed input.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** A create-order endpoint would declare that it accepts an idempotency key header, requires a valid request body, and returns 201 on success, 409 on duplicate key conflict, 429 on rate limit, and 422 on malformed input.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- - API design is about long-lived contracts, not endpoint naming alone.
- - Idempotency and pagination should be first-class concerns in write and list APIs.

## Alternatives considered

### Decision Guide: REST, RPC, and Contract Complexity

If you need protocol-level trade-offs, pair this post with System Design Protocols: REST, RPC, and TCP/UDP.


## Failure and degraded modes

### Pattern 1: Resource-first endpoint design

- **Detection:** Instead of action-heavy endpoints like /createOrder , design around resources: - POST /orders - GET /orders/{order id} - GET /orders?customer id=...
- **User or operator impact:** Instead of action-heavy endpoints like /createOrder , design around resources: - POST /orders - GET /orders/{order id} - GET /orders?customer id=...

### Pattern 2: Idempotent writes for retry safety

- **Detection:** Client retries are inevitable during network failures.
- **User or operator impact:** Client retries are inevitable during network failures.

### Pattern 3: Cursor-based pagination

- **Detection:** Offset pagination ( page=1000 ) becomes slow and unstable at scale.
- **User or operator impact:** Offset pagination ( page=1000 ) becomes slow and unstable at scale.

### Pattern 4: Structured errors

- **Detection:** Avoid free-form strings as your main failure contract.
- **User or operator impact:** Avoid free-form strings as your main failure contract.

### Trade-offs & Failure Modes: How API Contracts Break at Scale

- **Detection:** The best interview answer names at least one failure mode and one mitigation tied to API contract design.
- **User or operator impact:** The best interview answer names at least one failure mode and one mitigation tied to API contract design.

articles.contentMarkdown:
## Scenario context

SQL gives you ACID guarantees and powerful relational queries; NoSQL gives you horizontal scale and flexible schemas. The real decision is not "which is better" — it is "which trade-offs align with your workload." Understanding replication, sharding, and the CAP theorem helps you pick correctly every time.

---



```architecture
{
  "version": 1,
  "title": "TLDR:** SQL gives you ACID guarantees and powerful relati…

This walkthrough focuses on **SQL and NoSQL Engines: What Is Actually Inside**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- SQL internals SQL engines parse → plan → optimize → execute.
- - B-Tree indexes for range queries.
- - Hash indexes for equality lookups.

**Concepts in play:** consistency-replication, database-indexing, btree-vs-lsmtree, caching

## Scenario context

Caching is the single highest-leverage performance tool in distributed systems. This guide covers every read/write pattern (Cache-Aside through Refresh-Ahead), every eviction policy (LRU through ARC), cache invalidation pitfalls, thundering herd mitigations, multi-level topologies, and how Twitter, Netflix, and Facebook run caches at planetary scale. Read once; reference forever.

This walkthrough focuses on **Why Your Database Is Begging for a Cache**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Every relational database has the same story: it starts fast, traffic grows, queries get slower, you add indexes, you tune joins, and eventually you hit the wall — the database is doing too much I/O for too many concurr…
- The standard answer is a cache.
- A cache is a key-value store that lives in RAM.

**Concepts in play:** caching, consistency-replication, system-design-hld-architectures, database-indexing

## Stage 1 — How Caches Fit Into the Read and Write Path

- Before diving into patterns, ground yourself in what a cache is not: it is not a database.
- Caches are: - Volatile — data survives only as long as the cache process is running (unless persistence is explicitly configured, as in Redis RDB/AOF modes).
- - Bounded — caches have a fixed memory budget and cannot grow infinitely.
- When the budget fills, the eviction policy decides what to drop.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** When the budget fills, the eviction policy decides what to drop.

## Stage 2 — Every Cache Pattern Explained: From Cache-Aside to Refresh-Ahead

- There are six canonical caching patterns.
- Each solves a different problem and carries different consistency trade-offs.
- A typical production system mixes them — Cache-Aside for general reads, Write-Through for high-value writes, and Refresh-Ahead for peak-traffic hot keys.
- Pattern 1: Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) The most common pattern.

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

- The Internals: LRU, LFU, ARC, SLRU, and How They Actually Work When the cache is full and a new key must be inserted, the eviction policy selects the victim to remove.

- LRU — Least Recently Used The most widely deployed policy.
- Internally implemented as a doubly linked list + hash map : the hash map provides O(1) key lookup; the linked list maintains access recency from most-recent (head) to least-recent (tail).

- Twitter — Redis Sorted Sets for Timeline Assembly Twitter's home timeline is one of the most complex caching problems at scale.
- Assembling a feed from tens of thousands of followed accounts in real time would require expensive fan-in joins across hundreds of database shards on every page load.
- Instead, Twitter pre-computes each user's timeline and caches it in Redis as a sorted set (scores = tweet timestamps).

- - Write throughput overloads the primary.

## Scenario context

Short shareable IDs need Base62 (URL shorteners). Database primary keys at scale need time-ordered IDs (Snowflake, UUID v7). Security tokens need random IDs (UUID v4, NanoID). Picking the wrong strategy either causes B-tree fragmentation at 50M+ rows, production collisions, or IDs that leak your business metrics to competitors.



```architecture

This walkthrough focuses on **The Uniqueness Problem Hiding Inside Every Production System**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- You have 500 million shortened URLs.
- Every ID collision is a production incident — the wrong page opens for someone clicking a shared link.
- How do you guarantee uniqueness at scale while keeping IDs short enough for humans to share?

**Concepts in play:** api-gateway, caching, hash-tables-and-bloom-filters, database-indexing

## Stage 1 — What "Base" Actually Means — Encoding Numbers Into Shorter Strings

- "Base encoding" sounds cryptographic, but the concept is simple: you have a number, and you want to represent it using a given set of characters.
- The larger your character set, the fewer characters you need for the same numeric value.
- Think of it like counting in different number systems.
- Decimal (base-10) needs more digits than hexadecimal (base-16) to represent large numbers.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Decimal (base-10) needs more digits than hexadecimal (base-16) to represent large numbers.

## Stage 2 — How Each ID Strategy Generates Uniqueness at Scale

- Auto-Increment + Base Encoding The database sequence generates a monotonically increasing integer.
- The application encodes it in Base62 (or Base58) to produce a short, human-friendly string.
- Used by bit.ly and early YouTube.
- 6 chars of Base62 gives 56 billion unique IDs from a single counter.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

    Driver["Driver Node"]
    Planner["Query Planner"]
    Optimizer["Catalyst Optimizer"]
    Executor["Executor Task"]
    
    Driver -->|"Process Flow"| Planner
    Planner --> Optimizer
    Optimizer -->|"Optimized Plan"| Executor
    Executor -->|"Result"| Driver
```

**Observable outcome:** 6 chars of Base62 gives 56 billion unique IDs from a single counter.

## Stage 3 — Visualizing the URL Shortener Write Path with Bloom Filter Guard

- When a user submits a long URL, the system must generate a short ID, verify it has not been used before, and atomically store the mapping.
- A Bloom filter acts as a probabilistic pre-check that avoids a database roundtrip for the vast majority of new IDs — if the filter says "definitely not seen before," skip the DB check.
- If it says "possibly seen," fall back to the database.
- The diagram below shows the write path for a Base62 counter-based URL shortener.

*Applies **hash-tables-and-bloom-filters** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[User submits long URL] --> B[App Server]
    B --> C{Bloom Filter:  ID seen before?}
    C -->|Definitely not seen| D[Encode counter  Base62 short ID]
    C -->|Possibly seen  collision risk| E[Increment counter, get next ID]
    D --> F{DB unique constraint:  ID already exists?}
    F -->|ID is unique| G[Write mapping to DB]
    F -->|Collision confirmed| E
    G --> H[Add new ID to Bloom Filter]
    G --> I[Return short URL to user]
    E --> D

```

**Observable outcome:** The diagram below shows the write path for a Base62 counter-based URL shortener.

## Stage 4 — The URL Shortener Deep Dive — Making 500M Short Links Work Without a Single Collision

- URL shorteners are the canonical ID strategy interview problem because every constraint is concrete and measurable.
- Let us walk through the decision in order.
- Requirement baseline: 500M URLs total.
- At 6-char Base62: 62^6 = 56.8 billion possible IDs.

*Applies **database-indexing** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** At 6-char Base62: 62^6 = 56.8 billion possible IDs.

## Stage 5 — Choosing Your ID Strategy: Decision Flowchart and Use-Case Matrix

- The right strategy is determined by your constraints.
- Start from length, then sortability, then coordination model.
- This flowchart covers 95% of real-world decisions.
- When two strategies appear equal on the flowchart, prefer the one your database or ORM natively supports — operational familiarity reduces incident blast radius.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[What are your constraints?] --> B{Need short human-shareable IDs? 8 chars}
    B -->|Yes| C{Sortability required?}
    C -->|Yes| D[ULID or KSUID 2627 chars sortable]
    C -->|No| E[Base62 counter + Bloom filter]
    B -->|No  internal or longer OK| F{Need time-sorted IDs for DB performance?}
    F -->|Yes| G{Multi-node distributed?}
    G -->|Yes| H[Snowflake ID or UUID v7]
    G -->|No  single DB| I[UUID v7 or auto-increment]
    F -->|No sort needed| J{Content deduplication?}
    J -->|Yes| K[Truncated SHA-256  Base62]
    J -->|No| L{Security token? Must be unguessable}
    L -->|Yes| M[NanoID or UUID v4]
    L -->|No| N[UUID v4 is sufficient]
```

**Observable outcome:** When two strategies appear equal on the flowchart, prefer the one your database or ORM natively supports — operational familiarity reduces incident blast radius.

## Stage 6 — Sizing Your Namespace — The Birthday Paradox Applied to ID Collision Risk

- The birthday paradox reveals a counterintuitive truth: you do not need to fill a namespace before collisions become likely.
- You need roughly √(namespace size) records before the collision probability exceeds 50%.
- The approximation formula is: P(collision) ≈ n² / (2 × namespace size) Where n is the total number of IDs generated.
- Example: Base62 Namespace Collision Probability by Record Count The 6-char Base62 row reveals why the URL shortener must use 7 characters.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Example: Base62 Namespace Collision Probability by Record Count The 6-char Base62 row reveals why the URL shortener must use 7 characters.

## End-to-end outcome

You have 500 million shortened URLs.

## Alternatives considered

The source focuses on one primary design. A second architecture is not compared, so no alternative is invented here.

## Failure and degraded modes

### Random vs Time-Ordered: The Tradeoff That Breaks B-Tree Indexes in Production

- **Detection:** The most common production ID mistake is using UUID v4 as a primary key and discovering the performance cliff at 50–100M rows — by which point a schema migration is painful.
- **User or operator impact:** The most common production ID mistake is using UUID v4 as a primary key and discovering the performance cliff at 50–100M rows — by which point a schema migration is painful.

articles.title: Write-Time vs Read-Time Fan-Out: How Social Feeds Scale
articles.contentMarkdown:
## Scenario context

Fan-out is the act of distributing one post to many followers' feeds. Write-time fan-out (push) pre-computes feeds at post time — fast reads but catastrophic write amplification for celebrities. Read-time fan-out (pull) computes feeds on demand — no amplification but slow reads at scale. Production systems like Twitter/X, Instagram, and Facebook use a **hybrid**: write-time fan-out for users with ≤ 10K followers, re…

This walkthrough focuses on **The Social Feed Problem: One Post, Ten Million Inboxes**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- When Justin Bieber tweets, roughly 300 million accounts are eligible to see it.
- Your system has milliseconds to decide: do you immediately push that tweet into every follower's pre-built feed cache, or do you wait and assemble each follower's feed the moment they open the app?
- This is the fan-out problem — the act of distributing a single write event to many downstream consumers — and it is the central architectural decision in every social feed, notification system, and activity stream.

**Concepts in play:** caching, system-design-hld-architectures, database-indexing, event-driven-architecture

## Stage 1 — Deep Dive: Inside the Redis Feed Cache and the Async Fan-Out Pipeline

- The Internals: Redis Sorted Sets, Kafka Topics, and Fan-Out Workers The canonical feed cache data structure is a Redis sorted set ( ZSET ).
- Each follower's feed is stored as a key like feed:{userId} where each member is a postId and the score is the post's Unix timestamp in milliseconds.
- This enables: - ZADD feed:42 1711720800000 postId:9999 — insert a post reference - ZREVRANGE feed:42 0 49 WITHSCORES — fetch the 50 most recent posts - ZREMRANGEBYRANK feed:42 0 -501 — evict entries beyond a 500-post ca…
- Post content is fetched separately in a second read from a post cache or DB, allowing the feed cache to remain compact and fast.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```
Kafka Topic: post.created
  Partition key: authorId (ensures ordered delivery per author)
  Consumer Group 1: fan-out-workers (writes to Redis feed caches)
  Consumer Group 2: notification-workers (sends push notifications)
  Consumer Group 3: analytics-ingest (feeds the engagement pipeline)
```

**Observable outcome:** Post content is fetched separately in a second read from a post cache or DB, allowing the feed cache to remain compact and fast.

## Stage 2 — The Hybrid Architecture: Routing Posts by Follower Count

- The hybrid model routes the fan-out decision at post time, not at read time.
- The Fan-out Router — consuming from the post.created Kafka topic — checks the author's follower count against a configurable threshold (typically 10,000).
- Normal users fan out immediately; celebrity posts skip the write fan-out entirely and are stored in a dedicated Celebrity Post Store instead.
- The partition key for post.created should be authorId .

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

```java
@Configuration
public class FanOutKafkaConfig {

    @Bean
    public ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory<String, PostCreatedEvent> fanOutContainerFactory(
            ConsumerFactory<String, PostCreatedEvent> consumerFactory) {

        ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory<String, PostCreatedEvent> factory =
            new ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory<>();

        factory.setConsumerFactory(consumerFactory);
        factory.setConcurrency(8);             // 8 threads per pod, one per Kafka partition
        factory.getContainerProperties()
               .setAckMode(ContainerProperties.AckMode.MANUAL_IMMEDIATE); // Commit only after Redis write succeeds

        return factory;
    }
}

@Component
public class FanOutConsumer {

    @KafkaListener(
        topics = "post.created",
        groupId = "fan-out-workers",
        containerFactory = "fanOutContainerFactory"
    )
    public void consume(PostCreatedEvent event, Acknowledgment ack) {
        fanOutService.handlePostCreated(event);
        ack.acknowledge(); // Only commit offset once fan-out is complete
    }
}
```

**Observable outcome:** The partition key for post.created should be authorId .

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- Forgetting to handle the celebrity path during cold-start backfill.
- When a user's feed cache expires and is rebuilt from the post DB, it is easy to only restore write-time fan-out posts.
- - Write-time fan-out (push) pre-computes follower feeds at post time using Redis sorted sets.
- Reads are O(1) but writes are O(N followers).

## Alternatives considered

### Fan-Out Fundamentals: The Push vs. Pull Decision

Fan-out refers to the branching factor of a write event: when one user posts, the event must "fan out" to all followers who should see it.

### Write-Time Fan-Out: Paying the Cost at Post Time

When a user with 500 followers posts, a fan-out worker writes 500 entries into Redis — one per follower's sorted set feed cache — with the score set to the post's Unix timestamp.

### Read-Time Fan-Out: Paying the Cost at Read Time

Read-time fan-out inverts the model entirely.


## Failure and degraded modes

The source does not isolate a separate failure mode. Limits that matter for the scenario are called out in the stage decisions above.

articles.title: System Design Networking: DNS, CDNs, and Load Balancers
articles.contentMarkdown:
## Scenario context

When you hit a URL, **DNS** translates the name to an IP, **CDNs** serve static assets from the edge nearest to you, and **Load Balancers** spread traffic across many servers so no single machine becomes a bottleneck. These three layers are the traffic control system of the modern internet.

---

In 2021, GitHub went dark for nearly two hours. The cause was a misconfigured BGP route that blackholed traffic to GitHub…

This walkthrough focuses on **Three Layers That Stand Between a User and Your Server**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- In 2021, GitHub went dark for nearly two hours.
- The cause was a misconfigured BGP route that blackholed traffic to GitHub's DNS servers — meaning no request could resolve github.com to an IP address at all, let alone reach an application server.
- The outage was not a code bug or a database crash; it was a failure in the three infrastructure layers that execute before your application code ever runs.

**Concepts in play:** caching, system-design-hld-architectures, load-balancing, jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection

## Stage 1 — The Building Blocks: What Each Component Does

- Every web request to your application routes through three core network layers before reaching your code.
- DNS (Domain Name System) is the phone book of the internet: it translates human-readable hostnames like api.example.com into machine-readable IP addresses.
- Without DNS, users would need to memorize IP addresses directly to reach your service.
- CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a distributed cache of static assets.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** CDN (Content Delivery Network) is a distributed cache of static assets.

## Stage 2 — DNS: The Internet's Phone Book

- DNS maps example.com → 192.0.2.1 .
- The resolution chain has four hops: 1.
- Recursive resolver (usually your ISP or 8.8.8.8) receives the query.
- Root server directs to the TLD server.

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant OS as OS Cache
    participant RR as Recursive Resolver
    participant Root as Root NS (.)
    participant TLD as TLD NS (.com)
    participant Auth as Authoritative NS

    B->>OS: Resolve api.example.com
    OS-->>B: Cache miss
    B->>RR: Query api.example.com
    RR->>Root: Where is .com?
    Root-->>RR: TLD NS address for .com
    RR->>TLD: Where is example.com?
    TLD-->>RR: Auth NS for example.com
    RR->>Auth: A record for api.example.com?
    Auth-->>RR: 203.0.113.10 (TTL 300s)
    RR-->>B: 203.0.113.10 (cached per TTL)

```

**Observable outcome:** Root server directs to the TLD server.

## Stage 3 — CDNs: Bringing Content Closer to Users

- A CDN is a globally distributed cache.
- When a user requests /static/logo.png , the CDN serves it from an edge PoP (Point of Presence) in their city rather than your origin server in a distant datacenter.
- CDN hit ratio is the fraction of requests served from cache: $$ ext{Avg Latency} = r \cdot L ext{edge} + (1 - r) \cdot L ext{origin}$$ where $r$ is the hit ratio.
- Even improving $r$ from 0.80 to 0.95 dramatically reduces effective latency.

*Applies **load-balancing** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Even improving $r$ from 0.80 to 0.95 dramatically reduces effective latency.

## Stage 4 — Load Balancers: Distributing Traffic Intelligently

- A load balancer sits in front of your server pool and routes incoming requests: Layer 4 vs Layer 7: Routing algorithms: Health checks probe each backend (HTTP /health , TCP ping) on a configurable interval.
- Unhealthy servers are removed from rotation without human intervention.
- Load imbalance metric: $$ ext{Imbalance} = rac{\max( ext{server QPS})}{ ext{avg}( ext{server QPS})}$$ A ratio near 1.0 means excellent distribution; above 2.0 is a warning sign.
- 📊 CDN Cache Miss and Hit Flow This sequence diagram contrasts a CDN cache miss on the first request with a cache hit on the second request for the same static asset.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[User Browser] -->|DNS lookup returns LB IP| B[Load Balancer L7]
    B -->|Route /api| C[App Server 1]
    B -->|Route /api| D[App Server 2]
    B -->|Route /static| E[CDN Edge Node]
    C --> F[Origin DB]
    D --> F

```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant E as CDN Edge PoP
    participant O as Origin Server

    C->>E: GET /static/logo.png
    Note over E: Cache MISS (first request)
    E->>O: Forward to origin
    O-->>E: 200 OK + logo.png payload
    E-->>C: 200 OK (served + cached at edge)
    Note over E: Cached for max-age=86400s

    C->>E: GET /static/logo.png
    Note over E: Cache HIT
    E-->>C: 200 OK (from edge, ~5ms)
    Note over O: Origin not contacted on hit

```

**Observable outcome:** 📊 CDN Cache Miss and Hit Flow This sequence diagram contrasts a CDN cache miss on the first request with a cache hit on the second request for the same static asset.

## Stage 5 — Deep Dive: Inside a DNS Resolution and Cache Lifecycle

- When you type a URL, the OS checks its local DNS cache first.
- On a miss, the query travels to a recursive resolver, which fans out to root → TLD → authoritative nameserver.
- Each hop adds a few milliseconds — but the result is cached per TTL, so repeat visits skip all hops.
- This is why TTL tuning matters: a 24-hour TTL means stale IPs persist for 24 hours after a server change.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** This is why TTL tuning matters: a 24-hour TTL means stale IPs persist for 24 hours after a server change.

## Stage 6 — The Full Request Journey: DNS → CDN → Load Balancer → App

- This diagram shows how a single user interaction splits into two parallel paths: the API request travels through DNS resolution to the load balancer and then to an app server, while the static asset request is intercept…
- Notice that the CDN request never touches the load balancer or app server — this is the core value proposition of a CDN, removing an entire class of requests from the origin.
- The combined effect of DNS caching, edge caching, and load-balanced app servers is what allows a modest backend cluster to serve millions of users globally.

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User Browser
    participant R as Recursive Resolver
    participant A as Authoritative NS
    participant LB as Load Balancer
    participant CDN as CDN Edge
    participant App as App Server

    U->>R: Resolve example.com
    R->>A: Query A record
    A-->>R: Returns LB IP
    R-->>U: LB IP (cached per TTL)
    U->>LB: GET /api/data
    LB->>App: Forward request
    App-->>LB: JSON response
    LB-->>U: JSON response
    U->>CDN: GET /static/logo.png
    CDN-->>U: Serve from edge cache
```

**Observable outcome:** The combined effect of DNS caching, edge caching, and load-balanced app servers is what allows a modest backend cluster to serve millions of users globally.

## End-to-end outcome

Message queues and event-driven architecture let services communicate asynchronously, absorb bursty traffic, and isolate failures. The core design challenge is not adding a queue — it is defining delivery semantics, retry behavior, and idempotent consumers.






Queues are not a default replacement for APIs. They are a pressure-relief boundary when synchronous chains become fragile under burst traffic or partial ou…

This walkthrough focuses on **When to Use Event-Driven Queues and When Not To**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- When to use - Work is naturally asynchronous: notifications, enrichment, indexing, billing reconciliation.
- - Producer traffic is bursty, but outcomes can be delayed by seconds or minutes.

articles.title: System Design Service Discovery and Health Checks: Routing Traffic to Healthy Instances
articles.contentMarkdown:
## Scenario context

Service discovery is how clients find the right service instance at runtime, and health checks are how systems decide whether an instance should receive traffic. Together, they turn dynamic infrastructure from guesswork into deterministic routing.

> **TLDR**: If you scale beyond static IPs, discovery plus health-aware routing becomes a core reliability primitive.

In small systems, service communication can start w…

This walkthrough focuses on **Why Service Discovery Is the Invisible Backbone of Modern Systems**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- In small systems, service communication can start with fixed hostnames and static configuration.
- That model breaks quickly once autoscaling, rolling deploys, and multi-zone failover enter the picture.
- In production, service instances come and go all day: - New instances launch during traffic spikes.

**Concepts in play:** api-gateway, database-indexing, caching, canary-deployments

## Stage 1 — The Two Discovery Models You Must Distinguish in Interviews

- Service discovery usually appears in one of two patterns.
- Client-side discovery: the client queries a service registry and chooses a backend instance directly.
- This is common in microservice SDKs where clients include load-balancing logic.
- Server-side discovery: the client calls a stable endpoint (for example, a load balancer or API gateway), and that component resolves healthy backends.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Server-side discovery: the client calls a stable endpoint (for example, a load balancer or API gateway), and that component resolves healthy backends.

## Stage 2 — How Discovery and Health Checks Work End-to-End

- A robust discovery path is usually a loop, not a one-time lookup.
- Service instance starts and registers itself with metadata.
- Registry stores endpoint, zone, version, and status.
- Clients or proxies query for candidate instances.

*Applies **database-indexing** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Clients or proxies query for candidate instances.

## Stage 3 — Discovery Flow: Registration to Health-Aware Routing

- This model captures the key principle: discovery and health checks are continuous control loops, not setup-time configuration.
- 📊 Service Registration and Client Discovery This sequence diagram traces the full lifecycle of service registration and client-driven discovery.
- OrderService registers with the registry and sends heartbeats every 5 seconds to maintain its healthy status; when a Client queries for available endpoints, the registry returns only healthy instances, and the Client ro…
- Discovery is not a one-time lookup — it is a continuous health-maintained contract that ensures clients never route to stale or unhealthy backends.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```mermaid



flowchart TD
    A[Instance boots] --> B[Register with service registry]
    B --> C[Heartbeat and metadata updates]
    C --> D{Healthy and ready?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Add to routing pool]
    D -->|No| F[Exclude from routing pool]
    E --> G[Client or proxy resolves target]
    G --> H[Request served]
    F --> I[Recovery or restart]
    I --> C

```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as OrderService
    participant R as Service Registry
    participant C as Client
    S->>R: Register: host port tags
    R-->>S: ACK registration
    S->>R: Heartbeat every 5s
    C->>R: Discover order-service
    R-->>C: Return healthy endpoints
    C->>S: Route request
    S-->>C: Response

```

**Observable outcome:** Discovery is not a one-time lookup — it is a continuous health-maintained contract that ensures clients never route to stale or unhealthy backends.

## Stage 4 — Real-World Applications: API Gateways, Payments, and Internal Platforms

- HashiCorp Consul at scale: Consul's gossip protocol propagates health changes across a cluster in ~200ms on typical LAN deployments.
- The deregister critical service after field automatically removes services that remain unhealthy beyond a configurable window — preventing stale endpoints from silently accumulating in the registry.
- When a service registers with Consul, it provides its name, port, and metadata tags alongside a health check definition.
- The check specifies the HTTP path to poll, the polling interval, the per-check timeout, and — critically — a window after which Consul automatically deregisters a service that remains in a critical state.

*Applies **canary-deployments** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** The check specifies the HTTP path to poll, the polling interval, the per-check timeout, and — critically — a window after which Consul automatically deregisters a service that remains in a critical state.

## Stage 5 — Practical Example: Evolving a Checkout Service Beyond Static Backends

- Imagine a checkout service initially routed via hardcoded backend IPs.
- Problems appear during traffic spikes: - New app instances launch but receive no traffic.
- - One bad instance still receives requests for minutes.
- - Rolling deploys create intermittent errors from stale endpoint lists.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** - Rolling deploys create intermittent errors from stale endpoint lists.

## Stage 6 — Dynamic Registration and Health-Aware Discovery in Production

- Spring Cloud Netflix Eureka is a client-side service registry built into the Spring Cloud ecosystem; Spring Cloud Consul provides the same programming model backed by HashiCorp Consul's gossip-based registry.
- Both integrate with a discovery client abstraction and a health indicator framework to expose liveness and readiness semantics to the control plane automatically.
- How it works in practice: A microservice opts into dynamic discovery by declaring itself as a discovery client at startup.
- From that point, registration and heartbeat renewal happen automatically — the developer does not manage registry calls manually.

*Applies **database-indexing** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** From that point, registration and heartbeat renewal happen automatically — the developer does not manage registry calls manually.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- - Service discovery is a control-plane capability, not just a DNS trick.
- - Health checks must distinguish process liveness from real request readiness.

## Alternatives considered

### Decision Guide: Choosing a Discovery Strategy

When unsure in interviews, start with server-side discovery for simpler client behavior, then discuss where client-side control may be worth the complexity.


## Failure and degraded modes

### The Internals: Registries, Heartbeats, TTLs, and Routing Metadata

- **Detection:** Most systems maintain a control plane with these pieces: - Registry store for service instances and metadata.
- **User or operator impact:** Most systems maintain a control plane with these pieces: - Registry store for service instances and metadata.

Distributed caches trade strict consistency for sub-millisecond read latency, using consistent hashing to scale horizontally without causing database-shattering "cache stampedes" during cluster rebalancing.

**Concepts in play:** system-design-hld-architectures, caching, graph-traversal-algorithms, event-driven-architecture

## Stage 1 — News Feed: Use Cases, Actors, and Scale Requirements

- Actors - Publisher / Author: Creates and posts content (text, media).
- - Reader / Follower: Consumes a ranked home feed of followed users' posts.
- - System: Handles fan-out, ranking, and timeline materialization.
- Functional Requirements - Post Creation: Users can POST content with text/media.

## Stage 2 — Basics of News Feed Architecture

- At its heart, a news feed is a many-to-many relationship pipeline .
- Unlike a simple blog where one post is read by everyone, a feed is a personalized "inbox" for every user.
- Apache Kafka is the decoupling mechanism between post creation and fan-out.
- The posts.created topic is partitioned by author id , ensuring that all posts from one author are processed by the same fan-out worker partition and arrive in creation order.

- The Celebrity Threshold Requires Continuous Calibration.
- Setting the celebrity threshold too low pushes too many accounts into pull fan-out, degrading read performance for mid-tier influencers whose follower lists still take seconds to query.

## Scenario context

Payment systems optimize for correctness first, then throughput. This guide covers idempotency, double-entry ledgers, and reconciliation.

Stripe processes over 250 million API requests per day, and every single payment must be idempotent: a user clicking "Pay" twice must never produce two charges, even when the first HTTP call timed out and no confirmation reached the client. The Knight Capital incident of 2012 — w…

This walkthrough focuses on **Payment Processing: Use Cases & Requirements**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- A robust payment platform must handle several distinct user journeys and operational requirements.
- In an interview, defining these boundaries early is critical.
- Functional Requirements - Idempotent Authorization : Ensure that a payment request is processed exactly once, regardless of retries.

**Concepts in play:** system-design-hld-architectures, caching, consistency-replication, jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection

## Stage 1 — Basics: Baseline Architecture

- At its core, a payment system is a coordinator between three entities: the User (Client) , the Internal Ledger (Source of Truth) , and the External Payment Service Provider (PSP) .
- The baseline architecture consists of: 1.
- Payment API : The entry point that receives requests and orchestrates the flow.
- Idempotency Store : A fast, key-value store (like Redis) to track request keys.

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

## Stage 2 — Mechanics: Key Logic

- The most critical logic in a payment system is the Persist-Before-Call pattern combined with Double-Entry Bookkeeping .
- The Persist-Before-Call Pattern To prevent lost payments, you must record the intent to pay in your database before calling the external PSP.
- This ensures that if the call to the PSP times out or the server crashes, you have a record to reconcile against later.
- Double-Entry Bookkeeping Money is never simply "updated" in a row.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

    API->>Redis: Check existing key
    Redis-->>API: Not found — proceed
    API->>DB: Write PENDING intent
    DB-->>API: Intent persisted
    API->>PSP: Authorize charge with intent_id
    PSP-->>API: Authorization success
    API->>DB: Update status to AUTHORIZED
    API->>Redis: Cache response with 24h TTL
    API-->>U: Payment confirmed
```

**Observable outcome:** Double-Entry Bookkeeping Money is never simply "updated" in a row.

## Stage 3 — Estimations & Design Goals

- Before diving into the high-level design, let's establish the scale.
- - Throughput : 1,000 Transactions Per Second (TPS) average, 5,000 TPS peak (e.g., Black Friday).
- - Storage : Each transaction record is ~2KB.
- At 1,000 TPS, that's 2MB/sec, or ~172GB/day.

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** At 1,000 TPS, that's 2MB/sec, or ~172GB/day.

- The flow enforces the Persist-Before-Call pattern: the Payment API writes a PENDING intent record to the PostgreSQL ledger (step 2) before calling the external PSP (step 3).
- This ensures that even if the network drops between steps 3 and 4, the system has a record to reconcile against.
- The idempotency check in Redis (step 1) prevents a duplicate upstream call if the client retries with the same key.

## Stage 5 — Deep Dive: Double-Entry Bookkeeping, Idempotency Key Lifecycle, and the Reconciliation Engine

- Three mechanisms define correctness in a payment system: double-entry bookkeeping that makes every financial state change auditable, idempotency that prevents duplicate charges from network retries, and reconciliation t…
- Internals: Double-Entry Bookkeeping and Why Integer Cents Matter In a double-entry ledger, money is never simply "updated in a row." Every movement of value produces at minimum two ledger entries: a debit from one accou…
- When a customer pays $100 to a merchant, the system writes: DEBIT $100 from the customer's account, CREDIT $100 to the merchant's escrow account.
- The fundamental accounting invariant is that the sum of all debits must equal the sum of all credits across the entire ledger at all times.

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

    B -->|Yes| C["Return Cached Response Immediately"]

    E --> F["Call External PSP"]
    F --> G{"PSP Response Received?"}
    G -->|Success| H["Update Ledger to AUTHORIZED"]
    G -->|Failure| I["Update Ledger to FAILED"]
    H --> J["Cache Success Response — 24h TTL"]
    I --> J
    J --> K["Release Lock and Return to Caller"]
```

**Observable outcome:** The fundamental accounting invariant is that the sum of all debits must equal the sum of all credits across the entire ledger at all times.

## Stage 6 — Real-World Payment Architectures: Stripe, PayPal, and Square

- Stripe built its idempotency key system as a first-class API primitive from day one.
- Every write endpoint in the Stripe API accepts an Idempotency-Key header.
- Stripe stores the idempotency key, the request fingerprint (URL + body hash), and the response body in a dedicated idempotency database with a 24-hour retention window.
- Critically, Stripe validates that the same idempotency key is not used with a different request body — preventing a class of bugs where a client reuses a key across conceptually different operations.

### Trade-offs and Failure Modes in Payment System Design

- **Detection:** The Double-Charge Failure Mode: The API calls the PSP, the PSP charges the card and returns success, but the network drops before the response reaches the API.
- **User or operator impact:** The Double-Charge Failure Mode: The API calls the PSP, the PSP charges the card and returns success, but the network drops before the response reaches the API.
